extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of Stoic philosophy; readers seeking practical ethical guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines and evaluative criteria for living according to Epictetus/Stoic doctrine: what to value, how to act in relations and community, how to cultivate gratitude, acceptance (amor fati), and participation in Divine Intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontological Theorem — value only what is under your control
rubrics_metrics.description: The human being who places his good in things under his control, things that cannot in any way be suppressed and over which we have full responsibility, will be grateful to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing external things (those not under our control) leads to blaming others or God when they are lost, producing impiety and ingratitude. Therefore one must remove intrinsic value from externals and place the good in one’s own capacity for choice (prohairesis), judgment, desire, and related operations. Examples/anti-patterns: placing one's good in possessions, status, or people leads to revolt against the divine and ungrateful attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratitude presupposes correct application of the Ontological Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of giving thanks presupposes the correct application of the theorem regarding things that are under our control or not (Ontological Theorem), which leads us to the second premise: the human being who places his good in things under his control will be grateful to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gratitude follows from recognizing that what truly matters (and merits thanks) is what one can control — the cultivation and exercise of choice — rather than transitory externals. Rituals of thanks must therefore be grounded in correct valuation; otherwise gratitude is misdirected (e.g., thanking for worthless externals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the unimpeded capacity for choice as a gift (premise (3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The human being who recognizes that God has granted all humans the unimpeded capacity for choice will be grateful to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epictetus argues that assent and inclination toward truth are naturally unhindered and cannot be externally forced; recognizing this divine endowment fosters gratitude. Cultivate awareness that freedom of judgment/assent is an internal gift. Examples: one cannot be forced to accept falsehood as true; assent is internally governed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize Divine Providence in the things given for subsistence (premise (4))
rubrics_metrics.description: The human being capable of recognizing the Divine Providence in the things that have been given to him for the supply of his own life will be grateful to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External things, though not intrinsically valuable, together reveal Providence when seen in their interrelations (e.g., grass → sheep → milk → cheese). Developing the ability to see these connections (even by contemplating one relationship) enables proper gratitude and praise. Examples: hymns of thanks for mundane goods as evidence of Providence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for choice is naturally unimpeded — cultivate and exercise assent
rubrics_metrics.description: Man, you have the capacity for choice by nature unhindered and unconstrained ... Can anyone prevent you from inclining towards truth? No one can. Can anyone force you to accept falsehood? No one can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Epictetus’s argument about assent to ground personal responsibility: guard and educate your representations, desires, inclinations, and aversions because these internal faculties are the proper locus of moral value and action. The proof and practice involve training assent and resisting improper impulses by substituting other judgments or impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a comprehensive view of reality to perceive Providence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to develop the ability to see together the things that occur in the Cosmos ... external things reveal together the providence and goodness of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train to connect parts of reality (instrumental relations) so that even small examples (milk from pasture) reveal a providential order. You need not know every detail; contemplation of representative relations suffices. This fosters gratitude and the recognition of externals as instruments for exercising choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper ritual gratitude — observe ancestral customs within capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fitting for everyone to make libations, offer sacrifices, and first fruits according to ancestral custom, in a pure, diligent, not careless, not mean, and not beyond their capacity manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If performing ritual acts of thanks, do so sincerely and within your means. Rituals should not be careless, stingy, or exceed one’s capacity; their moral worth depends on correct valuation and intent rather than ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt cosmic citizenship — the human role of participating in Divine Intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the philosophers’ sayings about the kinship of gods and humans are true ... why do you yourself say you are Athenian and not just declare in which corner of the world your tiny body was thrown at birth? ... call yourself a 'citizen of the Cosmos' ... 'child of God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframe identity beyond narrow locality/particularity to see oneself as part of a rational whole sharing Divine Intelligence. This shift produces equanimity, benevolence, and a broad perspective on events and other people. Practice by cultivating the worldview of interconnection and shared rationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act appropriately (ta kathekonta) — measure actions by relations, not reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate actions are generally measured by relations. Is he your father? This implies taking care of him and tolerating him when he insults you ... maintain your own position in relation to him. So that your will is in accordance with nature, do not contemplate what he does, but what is given for you to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify your social/role-based relations (father, brother, citizen) and perform the duties that naturally attach to them. Avoid reactive retaliation; prefer to suffer wrongdoing rather than commit injustice. Practical method: determine the role and ask 'what falls to me to do here?' then act accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-as-play / Amor Fati — fulfill your assigned role skillfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that you are an actor in the play that the Master desires: if He wants it short, it will be short ... if He desires you to interpret the role of a beggar, it is for you to interpret that role skillfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept the circumstances and role assigned (birth, body, fortunes) and perform it well. Practice expressions/prayers of acceptance (Seneca/Arrian paraphrases) as reminders. Amor fati is attained by conforming one’s choice to divine desire; use recitation and reflection during hardship to cultivate this attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend concern through Hierocles’ concentric circles
rubrics_metrics.description: Each one of us is circumscribed by many circles ... the outermost and largest circle ... is that of the whole human race ... strive seriously to transfer oneself from comprehensive circles to the various individuals they comprehend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a deliberate effort to expand affection from the self and immediate family outward (call distant kin 'father/mother' etc.) and cultivate the Stoic discourse to replace natural partiality. Education and social practice (bringing people together) help form genuine bonds across wider circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anti-social actions; contribute to the common good by fulfilling roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-social actions include not only crimes listed in the penal codes, but also all kinds of attitudes that harm the common good ... The actions that collaborate for the common good are those undertaken by those who perceive themselves as true members of a community and include striving in their profession, their family roles ... and social roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions by whether they harm or help the polis/commonwealth. Small infractions (littering, rudeness) are morally relevant. Contribute through competent performance of your vocation and social duties (e.g., a baker running a good business that creates jobs and provides services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfill civic and professional roles with courage and integrity (Helvidius exemplar)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Vespasian sent him a request not to attend the Senate, Priscus replied: 'It depends on you not to allow me to be a senator. But, as far as I am one, I must attend.' ... 'Yours is condemning me to death. Mine is to die without trembling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplars: act according to role obligations even under threat; preserve moral stance and internal freedom. The rubric evaluates integrity (doing what you deem just in your office) and courage (meeting threats without fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice benevolence and charity; esteem benevolence as a chief virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: What virtue do we admire more than benevolence? ... Who should applaud more than us, the Stoics, who preach the brotherhood of the human race?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make benevolence a salient evaluative standard: cultivate charitable actions and attitudes toward others as central to Stoic life. This includes aiding family, friends, and community, and encouraging the brotherhood of humanity in speech and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate equanimity toward sickness, death, and misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not wish for events to happen as you wish, but wish for them to happen as they do, and your life will have a serene course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept natural facts (illness, death, misfortune) as part of being human and of the whole; do not take them as personal affronts. This disposition reduces anger and hatred and aligns will with divine nature. Practice by reframing events as role-appropriate occurrences (e.g., foot getting muddy) and by reminding yourself of the naturalness of such events.
